finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: attacker-controlled input in file causing printf to misinterpret data as a command
finding.assumptions: The attacker can control the content of the file, and the file content is treated as a command by printf.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Reviewed the code at line 18: `printf("Line: %s", buffer);`. The format string is a compile‑time constant and contains only the `%s` specifier, which safely prints the contents of `buffer` without interpreting it as a format string or shell command. No other function in the fragment processes `buffer` in a way that could lead to command execution. Thus, the untrusted data cannot reach an OS command execution sink.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: attacker-controlled input in file path causing processFile to misinterpret data as a command
finding.assumptions: The attacker can control the file paths returned by glob, and processFile treats these paths as commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the sink function processFile only performs a FILE* fopen and reads data with fgets; no system(), execve(), or other command execution calls are present. Also verified that the source globResult.gl_pathv[i] is passed directly to fopen, not to a command executor. The hardcoded search pattern in main ("*.txt") is not attacker‑controlled, so even if glob returned a path, it would only refer to a text file that the process can read. Therefore no OS command injection can occur.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: attacker-controlled input in file path causing processFile to misinterpret data as a command
finding.assumptions: The attacker can control the file paths returned by glob, and processFile treats these paths as commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked that the sink in processFile (lines 8-21) only performs fopen, fgets, and printf, with no system(), exec*, or other command‑execution calls. Also verified that the source globResult.gl_pathv[i] originates from globbing the hard‑coded pattern "*.txt" in main (line 40), so file paths are not attacker‑controlled. No neutralisation check is needed because the operation is not a command execution at all.

finding.title: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
finding.trigger: attacker-controlled input in file causing printf to misinterpret data as a command
finding.assumptions: The attacker can control the content of the file, and the file content is treated as a command by printf.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the printf usage on line 18: it uses a constant format string "Line: %s" and passes the file content as the %s argument. No format string specifiers are taken from the untrusted buffer, and the code does not invoke any shell or system call. Thus there is no path from the untrusted data to an OS command execution.
